posts.title: F3 Lightning: How Meta Accelerates Ads ML Features to Production at Scale
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Facebook Feature Framework (F3) is Meta’s framework for authoring, compiling, and serving the machine learning features underlying ads ranking models, where a single request can require more than 20,000 features. We first presented F3 at AI @ Scale 2020. 
F3 reduced execution computational costs by compiling all features into a single merged graph, but that graph also served as the release unit, so a single failure or invalid definition blocked the entire release pipeline.
This post introduces F3 Lightning, an infrastructure layer built on top of F3 to resolve this challenge by decoupling feature releases from shared execution, so each feature is compiled, validated, deployed, and rolled back independently.
The hardest part to solve was preserving F3’s efficiency improvements. Early per-feature release prototypes increased CPU usage because independent features no longer shared computation. We aimed to close this gap through four optimizations: stable computation identifiers, a single shared execution plan, one shared memory buffer across all features, and dense index mapping for direct array access.
With F3 Lightning, comparable extraction features now reach production ~3.6x faster than the prior F3, with no increase in infrastructure compute cost. This shorter release cycle also enables more model iterations in the same period.
A Primer on F3’s Shared Execution Architecture
Production machine learning systems rarely consume raw data directly. Before a model can make a prediction, its feature-serving system may need to read stored signals, filter events to a time window, count or sum values, normalize them, and combine intermediate results.
The simplest design to complete this work treats every feature as an independent function. That is easy to understand, but it becomes wasteful at scale, because features are not computationally independent. A seven-day click count and a seven-day impression count may read the same event source and apply the same time-window filter. A click-through rate feature may then reuse both results. Running each feature separately would repeat that filter, and every other shared step, on every request.
F3 approached this differently, by representing feature extraction as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each node performs one unit of work, such as reading an input, applying a filter, or calculating an aggregation. An edge means one computation depends on the result of another. The graph’s outputs are the feature values a model consumes.
Engineers author each feature independently in a high-level language. The F3 compiler turns each definition into a small graph, then merges the graphs for every feature a service uses into one merged graph (Figure 1). Where features share an operation, such as the seven-day filter above, the compiler collapses the duplicates into a single node. That shared work then runs once per request, not once for every feature that needs it. At runtime, feature extraction is a traversal of this merged graph.
Figure 1: F3 consolidates all features into one merged graph.
The Shared Graph Made Every Release All-or-Nothing
F3’s merged graph shared computation efficiently, but it came with a major catch: The graph was also the release, and one malformed definition could hold back every other feature in the merged graph.
Figure 2 illustrates this challenge. It shows seven independently authored features, A through G, where five definitions are valid, but D and G contain unrelated errors. The “Attempt 1” build fails on D, so none of the seven features ships. After D is corrected, the “Attempt 2” build reaches G and fails again. Only after both definitions are fixed in “Attempt 3” does the complete merged graph make it successfully to production.
Figure 2: One failing feature blocks the entire release.
Failures became more frequent as F3 scaled. F3 originally served a few hundred features, and at that size merges succeeded and releases were largely smooth. Today that number is more than 20,000, and different feature types need their own checks depending on how they compute, so new features and modified features are held to different testing bars. A feature that a model already consumes needs model-related tests before it can be released. Those tests are computationally expensive enough that they run only in a later release stage, and, because the merged graph ships as one unit, every other feature in it waits for them too.
F3 Lightning: Making Each Feature Its Own Release and Sharing Computation
After F3 launched, we made several rounds of improvements to the merged graph. Each one brought back release speed for a while, but the gains eroded as more features landed, because all features still shipped together in the merged graph. So F3 Lightning was built to make every feature releasable on its own while preserving F3’s efficiency. 

As illustrated in Figure 3, F3 Lightning introduced two changes to help achieve this:
Deployment granularity: Each feature is an independently releasable configuration. It is validated, shipped, and rolled back without affecting any other feature.
Efficiency parity: F3’s efficiency came from the merged graph, so giving every feature its own release removes the source of it. Matching that efficiency while keeping per-feature releases required several key optimizations in how F3 Lightning executes.
Figure 3: F3 Lightning separates the release boundary from the execution boundary.
Deployment Granularity: How F3 Lightning Isolates Feature Releases
Isolation starts in the compiler, where each feature is compiled on its own into a single configuration. That feature configuration carries everything needed to extract that feature — every node it needs, in order, with nothing borrowed from a neighbor. If feature C has a problem, feature A still ships, because the two configurations have no relationship to each other.
Figure 4: A bad feature no longer blocks a good one.
Because features are no longer merged at release time, each one can be selected and released on its own schedule. The release path becomes an ordered queue instead of a batch that ships all at once or not at all. Changes are prioritized by what they unblock. A new feature that no model consumes yet can go out quickly on standard validation, while a change to a feature a live model already reads gets extra testing first.
Figure 5: Features are selected from a priority queue by impact and risk.
Efficiency Parity: How F3 Lightning Preserved F3’s Serving Efficiency
Our first prototypes separated deployment only. Features shipped independently, but execution was no longer shared, so the prototypes used substantially more CPU than traditional F3. Each independently released configuration arrived at the serving process as its own graph and was executed separately, repeating every read, filter, and aggregation that F3’s merged graph had eliminated.
The fix was to bring shared execution back without bringing the merge back. At startup, F3 Lightning does not rebuild a merged graph. It takes the active feature configurations, consolidates the work they share, and arranges it into a single execution order. Getting back to parity took four steps: a compiler prerequisite followed by three startup optimizations.
Step 1: Stable Identifiers Make Shared Work Recognizable
To deduplicate execution, the runtime must recognize when two independently compiled configurations contain the same computation. Node numbers can’t do this, because numbering is local to each feature’s graph. The same seven-day filter might be node 2 in one configuration and node 7 in another, and inserting a single node renumbers everything after it. Traditional F3 never had this problem, because one compiler run saw every feature and could assign identifiers globally.
F3 Lightning instead has the compiler derive each identifier from what the work does, not where it sits: the operation, its parameters, and the identifiers of its inputs (see Figure 6). Because each input’s identifier already reflects everything upstream of it, the identifier captures the whole chain of work that produced the result. Where input order doesn’t affect the result, inputs are put in a standard order. Aggregations also include the properties that define their behavior, such as the time window and grouping keys. As a result, two features that define the same operation over the same inputs receive the same identifier, even if they were compiled and released weeks apart. If a computation’s meaning changes, its identifier changes with it.
Figure 6: The same computation gets the same identifier.
Step 2: One Execution Plan Across Every Feature
At service startup, F3 Lightning builds a single execution plan across all active features, using a topological sort to place every node after the nodes it depends on. When several features contain a node with the same identifier, the plan keeps one copy and connects every consumer to it, so that computation runs once no matter how many features use it.
Merging guarantees each computation runs once, but the plan is still a graph that the executor walks pointer by pointer on every request. The same startup pass therefore flattens it into an ordered list, so each request runs a single forward pass down the list instead of traversing a graph.
Sharing one plan raises a risk: A single failing computation could affect every feature. To prevent this, if a computation fails or its input is unavailable, F3 Lightning marks everything downstream of it as not ready, and the executor skips that work. A failure affects only the nodes that depend on it, and independent branches keep running.

Step 3: A Shared Memory Buffer, Because Deduplication Was Not Enough
After steps 1 and 2 were complete, no computation ran twice, yet CPU use was still above traditional F3. The remaining compute cost came from memory layout. Each configuration carried its own request-time data container, so intermediate results were scattered across separate memory allocations. Walking the plan in order meant jumping between them, and each jump cost a cache miss.
F3 Lightning replaced those per-feature containers with one buffer per request. At startup, each feature’s references are rebound to slots in that buffer. 

Three improvements follow from the single buffer:
Locality: Consecutive plan steps now touch adjacent memory, so the values a step reads are usually already in cache. This restores the sequential access pattern the merged graph always had. It also removes the per-feature allocation on every request.
One readiness vector: A single vector, stored apart from the values, replaces per-feature tracking, so the executor can check whether a value is ready without reading the value itself. The marker has to be separate because an empty list is a valid result, so “empty” can’t also mean “not computed yet.”
No duplicate copies: Most feature values are lists and maps, and consumers no longer get their own copy. The shared slot holds a reference to the producer’s result, so a computation used by 20 features is computed once and stored once. Single values (scalars) are still copied, because copying a small value is cheaper than following a pointer. This is safe because each buffer lasts only for one request, and the execution order guarantees each result outlives its last reader.
Figure 8: All features share one memory buffer.
Step 4: Dense Index Mapping Removes the Last Per-Access Cost
Values now lived together, but finding one was still computationally expensive. Every access had to resolve an identifier, which meant hashing a key, probing buckets, and following a pointer. Lookups weren’t computationally efficient at Meta’s serving volume. 
The final fix applied the same principle as steps 2 and 3, doing the work once at startup. F3 Lightning assigns every unique identifier a consecutive integer slot and rewrites every reference in every configuration to point at those slots, so identifiers are used only during initialization. Reading a result becomes a direct array index into the shared buffer, with no hashing and no lookup table on the request path.

With F3 Lightning, comparable extraction features now reach production ~3.6x faster than on traditional F3, with no increase in infrastructure computational cost. That shorter release cycle means models can be improved and retrained more often in the same period. Building F3 Lightning also taught us three lessons:
Deployment and execution should have separate boundaries: If one artifact determines both how components run and when they ship, a failure in any one of them blocks all the others. Splitting the two jobs removed a trade-off between efficiency and release speed.
Work that never changes between requests belongs at startup, not on the request path: Three tasks were identical for every request: spotting shared work, deciding the order to run it in, and finding where each result is stored. F3 Lightning now does them once, when the service starts, so independent releases add no computational cost to individual requests.
Two designs can execute the same operations in the same order and still differ substantially in CPU computational cost: In F3 Lightning, we removed every repeated computation, yet CPU use stayed above traditional F3. Each feature still kept its own copy of the shared results, spread across memory. Consolidating them into one copy per result closed the gap. This is the least obvious result in the project and the one that generalizes furthest. On modern CPUs, where results live and how many copies exist can matter as much as how many computations run.
Acknowledgments
We would like to thank Sourabh Bansal, Ping Chen, Weitao Chen, Benjamin Dummitt, Junhua Gu, Henry Hu, Jing Huo, Joffrey Liu, Rocky Liu, Weixi Ma, Shuby Mao, Sandeep Pandey, Mihir Rastogi, Tim Sombuntham, Matt Steiner, Vivienne Sung, Ritwik Tewari, Vivek Trehan, Arnaud Venet, Ziheng Wang, Gautam Wilkins, Fan Yang, Qiao Yang, Jie Zheng and the entire team behind the development and productionization of F3, Meta’s Ads ML feature computation and serving platform, and F3 Lightning, the capability built on top of it.

posts.title: IntelliJ Scala Plugin 2026.3 Is Out!
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Hello everyone!
Scala plugin 2026.3 is here! This release brings more accurate Scala 3 code analysis, substantially reworked Twirl support for Play Framework developers, and more efficient compiler-based highlighting that reduces redundant background work. You’ll also find improvements to build-tool support, debugging, and everyday editing. Let’s take a closer look at what’s new.
Scala 3
This release adds support for Scala 3.10 and improves built-in Scala 3 code analysis, reducing false errors and making inferred types more accurate.
Extension methods now resolve more accurately when overloads involve different or generic receiver types, method type parameters, or implicit conversions. We’ve also corrected resolution of right-associative extension operators. Code completion, navigation, and Quick Documentation distinguish extension methods with different receiver types more clearly, and code completion lists fewer duplicate entries.
Contextual argument resolution now makes better use of method arguments and explicit type arguments when selecting given instances. This avoids false ambiguity and missing-implicit errors in generic code, including calls where type and value parameter lists alternate.
Type inference now handles transparent traits more accurately, avoiding overly restrictive collection types. We’ve also improved inference involving higher-kinded type parameters and their bounds. For anonymous classes, we’ve corrected cases where the plugin inferred structural types that the compiler does not infer.






Improved Twirl support for Play Framework
We’ve substantially reworked Twirl template support for the Play Framework, starting with a complete architectural rewrite. We followed this with extensive improvements to parsing, code completion, formatting, Find Usages, and reference resolution. Together, these updates significantly reduce false errors while making editing, navigating, and refactoring templates more reliable.
Find Usages now reliably locates the Scala code that renders a particular template before you modify it. Renaming a template automatically updates references to it across your project, keeping call sites consistent when you reorganize your Play application.
The rewrite also reduces false errors within embedded HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and JSON. Combined with the formatting and completion enhancements, working with mixed-language templates is now much easier – with fewer misleading diagnostics interrupting your work.







Build-tool improvements: sbt, Scala CLI, and BSP
In Scala plugin 2024.3, we introduced separate main and test modules to better reflect sbt’s project structure. In 2026.3, this is the only supported layout, and the option to disable it has been removed. This layout supports more accurate dependency handling and different compiler options for main and test sources.
Importing sbt 2.x projects has also improved, specifically around compiler-plugin path resolution. In addition, build-script analysis now handles .value and / expressions correctly, preventing valid settings from being flagged as unresolved errors in the editor.
Performance-wise, we’ve addressed slow project imports with Scala 3.8, as well as a BSP import performance regression.
When a Scala 3 macro implementation changes, IDE builds now automatically recompile code that depends on it when necessary. This ensures compiled code no longer retains stale macro expansions after the macro implementation changes.
Dependency-coordinate completion is back for both sbt build definitions and Scala CLI //> using dep directives. When adding a library, code completion suggestions help you quickly find the correct coordinates and insert them into your build or script.
Finally, Scala CLI scripts now benefit from improved shebang parsing, highlighting, and formatting. An inspection detects missing execute permissions in local scripts with a first-line shebang and provides a quick-fix to make them executable, allowing you to resolve the issue before running the script directly.






Debugging improvements
You can now place breakpoints on single-line conditional return statements in ordinary methods, such as if (done) return result, and stop at those statements while debugging. We’ve also resolved issues where breakpoints were skipped inside Future callbacks and within for comprehensions defined in Scala 3 top-level methods.
Inspecting state in a paused program is also significantly smoother. We’ve resolved UI freezes during expression completion and watch evaluation, fixed an issue where object expansion got stuck on Collecting data, and corrected problems with the Initialize action for lazy val declarations.
Stopping at a breakpoint on a single-line conditional return.



More efficient compiler-based highlighting
Compiler-based highlighting now avoids unnecessary recompilations by reusing valid diagnostics, even for files closed during compilation. Switching tabs or reopening a file that has already been checked displays the stored results. In addition, typing triggers less background work, and pending checks across multiple files are now combined into a single compilation run.
Navigating between files in a failing module no longer triggers repeated compilation attempts while the project remains unchanged. Furthermore, if errors in another module block highlighting, the editor explains the cause and provides a link to the blocking errors.
Finally, we’ve resolved several edge-case issues. Multi-module BSP compilations no longer unexpectedly skip all targets, diagnostics are no longer shifted to incorrect lines when edits occur during compilation, and highlighting errors are no longer left hidden if a compilation run is canceled.
Identifying the module blocking compiler-based highlighting.



Smaller improvements in the editor
For a quicker look at inferred information, X-Ray mode now displays inferred type arguments for parameterless methods.
Go to Code | Desugar Scala Code to inspect Scala code with implicit and syntactic details expanded explicitly. For compiled Scala 3 classes, a new side-by-side view lets you compare the compiler’s interpretation with the plugin’s. This is especially useful when exploring code that relies heavily on implicit arguments or complex language constructs whose expanded forms are hard to discern from the source alone.
We’ve also resolved key formatting issues. We fixed a bug where formatting valid Scala 3 lambdas returning tuples in indentation syntax resulted in uncompilable code. We updated the integration with Scalafmt, and we corrected range formatting for partial selections and empty case bodies.
Compatibility changes and removals
Please review these changes before upgrading an existing setup:
Ammonite: We’ve removed dedicated script support, including Ammonite run configurations and $file/$ivy assistance. You can still run Ammonite scripts externally.
Fastpass: Fastpass integration is no longer available for project imports.
sbt module layout: Projects now use separate main and test modules, even where this mode was previously disabled. The setting to disable separate modules has been removed.
IntelliJ Scala Bundle: The experimental standalone distribution has been retired. Please install IntelliJ IDEA and the Scala plugin separately.
For plugin developers
The Scala plugin itself is now written in Scala 3. This internal migration requires no changes to the projects you open in IntelliJ IDEA. You can continue using their existing Scala versions and build configurations.
If you develop an IntelliJ IDEA plugin that compiles against Scala plugin APIs, rebuild it against your target Scala plugin 2026.3 build and verify compatibility with the updated API signatures and bundled dependencies. The API and dependency compatibility guide provides migration instructions.




IntelliJ IDEA 2026.3 also brings new features, performance improvements, and usability updates. Explore these changes in our What’s New and What’s Fixed posts.
As always, we welcome your feedback! Please report any issues you find on YouTrack, and feel free to ask questions or share your thoughts on Discord.
Happy developing!
The Scala team at JetBrains

posts.title: GoLand’s Profiler Now Works With AI Agents
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
In our practical guide to profiling in Go, we mentioned that some of the Go developers we talked to avoid pprof if they can. For many of them, typical Go services perform well enough without optimizations, so when they do need to profile, it can feel like a “rescue mission” with a tool they are not really experienced with. They have to remember which profile to take and how to collect it, and then make sense of a lot of low-level data.
GoLand 2026.1.2 made the collecting part easier with a built-in profiler. In GoLand 2026.3, we are taking it a step further – your AI agent can now use that profiler too. You describe the symptom, for example, “reindexing through POST /reindex takes much longer than it should, profile it”, and the agent runs your app with the profiler, picks the profiles that fit the problem, reads the results, and points you to the code that is responsible. You do not need to know what a mutex profile is or which pprof flags to pass.
This works with Claude Code, Codex, and Junie through the bundled goland-profiler skill and a set of MCP tools. Below, we take a closer look at what the agent does and how you can split the work with it.




What happens when you ask the agent to profile your app?
The goland-profiler skill tells the agent when to reach for the profiler, for example, for slow execution, high CPU usage, excessive allocations, memory growth, blocking, lock contention, or goroutine leaks. It also explains how to work with the MCP tools that give the agent access to GoLand’s profiler. A typical run goes like this:
Run with the profiler: If you have already started the app with the profiler, the agent reuses that run. Otherwise, it starts the app with the profiler using your run configuration, just as you would with the Run with Profiler button. The skill explicitly tells the agent not to add net/http/pprof or any temporary profiling code, so your source code stays untouched. If it is unclear whether the app is doing what it should, the agent can also read its output.
Pick the profile: The skill instructs the agent to take the narrowest capture that answers the question. For CPU issues, that means recording while it runs a workload, such as a load generator, or taking a timed profile if the load is steady. For other problems, it takes a block profile for synchronization waits, a mutex profile for lock contention, or two heap profiles to compare when memory keeps growing. Allocs, goroutine, and goroutine leak profiles are available too.
Read the results: Each capture comes back with a summary of up to five of the hottest functions in your code, showing where their cost goes, which lines are the most expensive, and how they are reached. The agent starts from this summary and only asks for more detail – the top functions under a given root, the call paths to a function, or the most expensive lines in a function – when the summary is not enough.
Report the findings: The agent tells you what the main bottleneck is and how much it costs, which call path in your code leads to it, where the hot lines are, and whether it is CPU work, allocations, blocking, contention, or goroutine growth. It also suggests a fix or a further measurement, and it is instructed to separate what the profile shows from its own hypotheses. If you ask, it can make the change too.
Every profile the agent captures ends up in the profiler session and in Recent profiles in the Go Optimization tool window, just like the ones you capture yourself. If you want to double-check the agent’s conclusion, you can open the same profile and look at the flame graph.
MCP tools
What the agent can do with GoLand’s profiler


Run the app with the profiler
Starts and stops your app with the profiler, the same way the Run with Profiler button does. Your source code is not changed.
run_with_profiler
Launches a run configuration with the profiler enabled.

list_profiled_runs
Lists active and recently stopped profiled runs, including the ones you started from the IDE.

get_profiled_run_output
Returns the program output of a profiled run, such as the app’s logs.

stop_profiled_run
Stops the profiled application.


Capture profiles
Saves captured profiles to the session and to Recent profiles, so you can open them in GoLand later.
take_profile
Captures a profile (a snapshot, or a CPU profile for a set duration) and returns it with a summary.

start_cpu_recording
Starts a CPU recording.

stop_cpu_recording
Stops the recording, saves the CPU profile, and returns a summary.


Read profiles
Works with any profile – one the agent captured, one you captured, or the one currently open in the editor.
list_profiles
Lists session, recent, and currently open profiles.

profile_summary
Returns totals and the top 5 functions with their hot lines and call paths, for any saved profile.

profile_top_frames
Ranks functions by self or cumulative cost, similar to pprof -top.

profile_call_paths
Shows the call paths that lead to a given function.

profile_source_lines
Ranks the source lines of a function by cost, similar to pprof -list.







How to split the work with the agent
How much of the process you hand over is up to you. These are the three setups we have found most useful:
The agent does everything: You describe the problem, and the agent handles the rest, from launching the app to explaining the results. This is a good option when you do not know where to start.
You profile, the agent analyzes: You run the profiler yourself, open a profile, and ask the agent what it sees. The agent can read the profile that is currently open, so there is nothing to export or describe.
You run the app, the agent captures: You start the app with the profiler and get it into the state you care about, for example, after a warm-up or with a production-like dataset loaded, and then ask the agent to take the profiles.
Workflows
Three ways to split the work with the agent


The agent does everything
Useful when you know something is slow but have no idea where to start.

1 You
“Reindexing through POST /reindex takes much longer than it should. Profile the app and tell me why.”

2 Agent
Loads goland-profiler, picks a run configuration, and calls run_with_profiler.
Your code stays as it is.


3 Agent
Sends some load to the app, records CPU with start_cpu_recording and stop_cpu_recording, and takes a heap or allocs profile if the symptom points to memory.
Each capture returns a summary with the hottest functions and call paths.


4 Agent
If the summary is not enough, digs deeper with profile_top_frames, profile_call_paths, or profile_source_lines, then stops the app it launched.

5 Agent
Explains what is slow and why, and can fix it if you ask.
The profiles stay in GoLand, so you can open them and check.


You profile, the agent analyzes
You stay in control of the run, and the agent helps you make sense of the profile you already have open.

1 You
Run the app with the profiler, reproduce the slow request, and capture a profile the usual way.

2 You
Open the profile. Something in the flame graph looks off, but you are not sure what.

3 You
“Look at the open profile. Why are we allocating so much?”

4 Agent
Finds the open profile through list_profiles, reads it with profile_summary, and goes deeper with profile_top_frames, profile_call_paths, or profile_source_lines if the summary is not enough.
It reads the same profile you are looking at.


5 Agent
Explains the hot path in terms of your code and suggests a fix.


You run the app, the agent captures
You start the app with the profiler and get it into the state you care about, and the agent takes it from there.

1 You
Start the app with the profiler and get it into the right state, for example, after a warm-up or with a production-like dataset loaded.

2 You
“It is running with the profiler now. Capture goroutine and mutex profiles and tell me where the contention is.”

3 Agent
Finds your run with list_profiled_runs, then calls take_profile for each profile type.

4 Agent
Reads the profiles, checks them against the source code, and reports back.
The app keeps running until you stop it.







Current limitations
GoLand-started app: GoLand’s profiler modifies the executable during compilation to expose the profiling API, so it cannot be attached to an already running process. The agent either starts the app through a run configuration with the profiler or works with a session you started yourself.
Short-lived programs: The profiler samples a running process, so a CLI tool that finishes in a fraction of a second does not leave enough time to capture anything useful. The skill works best for servers, workers, and other long-running services.
Tested agents: We have tested the workflow with Claude Code, Codex, and Junie. Other agents that can connect to GoLand’s MCP server may work too, but we have not verified them yet.
How to try it
Update to GoLand 2026.3 and open your project.
Make sure goland-profiler is enabled in Settings | AI | Skills. You can also restrict it to specific projects or turn it off there.
Ask your agent to profile your app, or open a profile you have captured and ask the agent what it sees.
Tell us what you think
We hope this makes profiling something you can do as part of your everyday work, and not only when a service is already in trouble. If you have been avoiding the profiler, this might be a good time to give it a try.
Download GoLand




We would love to hear how it works for you – which setup you end up using, whether the agent’s summaries are enough or you still open the flame graph, and which projects it does not work for. Feel free to tag us on X, drop into the #goland-gophers Slack channel, or create a ticket in our YouTrack issue tracker..
Happy coding,
The GoLand team

posts.title: Java Annotated Monthly – November 2026
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
October kept the Java world busy, with JDK news, fresh tutorials, Kotlin updates, AI experiments, and plenty more from across the wider ecosystem. We’ve gathered the best of it in one place, so you can skip the scrolling and get straight to the good stuff. To top it all off, Piotr Przybył joins us as this month’s featured guest.
Let’s go!
Featured Content
Piotr Przybył
Piotr Przybył  – Notorious engineer at work and after hours, tracing the meanders of the art of software engineering. Remote Software Gardener, mostly working in web-oriented Java gardens. Java Champion. Docker Captain. Testcontainers Champion. Programming usually in Java (since 1.3), Scala, and Go, but in other languages too. Fan of agility, seen mostly as choosing the right tools and approaches after asking the right questions. Developer, trainer, and conference speaker, currently working at Elastic as a Senior Developer Advocate.
Greetings, fellow Java developers! It’s a pleasure to be here again – it’s been three Java releases since the last time. We all know that means roughly 18 months, don’t we? ;-)
Both the world and our ecosystem were moving fast back then, and it seems they have only accelerated. This means one thing: good luck trying to keep up to date with everything. Luckily for us all, newsletters like this one help.
The autumn conference season of 2026 is slowing down. It was a busy and exciting one, for me in particular, because Java 28 is already shaping up. And if you look at the list of JEPs already there, how can you not be excited? Structured Concurrency is set to become final in March 2027, yay! Bye-bye, CompletableFuture, it was fun knowing you… not ;-). CF isn’t going anywhere, but it won’t be the best abstraction for concurrent subtasks. 
Apart from that, there’s going to be one less thing for me to rant about, because Java is going to have (for now as an incubator module) a Simple JSON API. If your microservice only has to send one simple REST request with a JSON body, maybe this plus the JDK’s HTTP client will be enough? You can learn about it from Dan Vega.
There are going to be improvements to GCs and more performance goodies, but my personal favourite is going to be Value Objects, because 42 is always 42, and it shouldn’t need an identity crisis to answer everything. I believe VOs will change the way we think about and work with data in Java. The need for this improvement is already here, because AI, like it or not, also means exchanging an awful lot of tokens and vectors.




To give you a taste of that, the following code yields different results on a default HotSpot configuration, with and without the value-object preview enabled:
Integer x = 1024, y = 1024; IO.println(x == y)
Intrigued? For more, please check out my post Java isn’t dead yet, but it can’t avoid Valhalla.
You may say, “Okay, but these are preview features or incubator modules; they can’t be used in production.” That’s not a blanket rule, although compatibility and support deserve a closer look. Sometimes even a non-GA feature of Java can be mature and worthwhile enough for you to make it a part of your library and code. I’m talking about the Vector API already being used in Lucene and Elasticsearch, and you can learn more about how it powers semantic search in them in one of my recent talks. If you prefer reading about SIMD, Krzysztof Ślusarski has you covered with this post.
I could go on and on about the exciting stuff in recent and upcoming Java releases. Marit van Dijk and I weren’t quite able to curb our enthusiasm for them, as can be seen in  this three-hour-long deep dive from Devoxx Belgium 😅. (We simply forgot to take a break, sorry!)
If you can spare just one hour, here’s a shorter and more compact version from Hello Stavanger.
A big congrats to Marit, my partner on stage, for becoming the most ubiquitous Java speaker for 2026!

posts.title: The Kotlin Multiplatform Contest Is Open: Win a Trip to KotlinConf
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
The Kotlin Multiplatform Contest is back! 
Students and recent graduates, turn your idea into a cross-platform project with Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP). 
The authors of the top three projects will each win a trip to KotlinConf 2027 in Kraków, Poland, with conference tickets, travel, and accommodation covered by the Kotlin Foundation. Authors of all other valid entries will receive Kotlin souvenirs.
Submissions are open until December 7, 2026.
Join the contest
Your project can be a game, a developer utility, a productivity app, an experiment with AI, or something entirely different. It needs to be created specifically for the contest, use KMP, and run on at least two platforms. Target Android, iOS, desktop, web, backend, or beyond.
Last year, we received 88 submissions, with 76 eligible entries from more than 30 countries. Participants built everything from AI-powered learning tools to social-impact projects and accessibility apps.
We can’t wait to see what you build this year!
Important dates
Submission deadline: December 7, 2026, 23:59 CET
Winners announced: December 21, 2026
KotlinConf 2027: April 22–23, 2027, Kraków, Poland
For the official rules on eligibility, submission, and prize conditions, see here.
Have questions or need help? 
Join the KMP Contest Slack channel to ask questions, follow contest updates, and connect with other participants and Kotlin experts.
Join the KMP Contest Slack channel →
Start here
You don’t need to know KMP before entering. This year’s contest page includes resources to help you get started, including the new KMP Contest Starter Kit.
The starter kit is an open-source starting point for developers new to KMP. It provides an AI-assisted path from idea to app, with ready-to-use agent skills, prompts, and workflows designed to help you build and test your applications. It complements the official KMP documentation.
Other resources include:
Kotlin Multiplatform learning resources.
PeopleInSpace: Multiplatform sample projects.
Kotlin AI examples.
Join the contest
What previous participants built
Over the past four years, participants have built projects spanning education, health and well-being, sustainability, developer tools, games, and plenty of unexpected ideas.
Here are just a few of the things they’ve built:
🧑‍🌾 AI assistant for farmers.
🛗 Office elevator controller.
🛟 Flood rescue device.
🎹 Synthesizer that lets you hear mathematical equations.
🤖 Robot control app.
🐣 Egg encyclopedia.
🏓 Game that turns your phone into a ping-pong racket.
Your project doesn’t need to fit a particular category. Build something you find useful, interesting, or simply fun, and use KMP to bring it to life across platforms.
What previous winners say
“You don’t need to be a Kotlin expert to enter; I definitely wasn’t. Kotlin Multiplatform let me share almost everything across Android and iOS, and still go native where it mattered. That’s what turned an idea into something real.” – Javier Quilumba
“The contest was a really good excuse to push myself and see how far I could take Kotlin Multiplatform with an actual product, rather than just experimenting with it.” – Tochukwu Adrian Ikeaba
“Kotlin Multiplatform showed me that you can just start building things. It became a starting point for many of my later projects, helped me explore new technologies, and the trip to KotlinConf was truly inspiring.” – Valerii Ovchinnikov
“Winning the contest and traveling to KotlinConf was an incredible experience. It gave me the opportunity to connect with the community and learn directly from industry experts.” – Mikołaj Lemański
“To me, it was important that I managed to do something I was proud of and learn something along the way.” – Andreea-Ștefana Vrabie
Ready to build?
You have until December 7 to take an idea, turn it into a KMP project, and submit it. 
Build across platforms. Experiment with something new. And perhaps we’ll see you at KotlinConf 2027 in Kraków!

posts.title: RustRover 2026.3 Is Out: JetBrains Air, Clearer Debugger Views, and Agents That Debug With You
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Fixing a bug starts with understanding what your code is doing at runtime: reading the program state, following the call stack, or tracking down a slow function. RustRover 2026.3 makes that work easier to follow, whether you do it yourself or with an AI agent. It also ships with JetBrains Air, a new layer for running coding agents and reviewing their work in the IDE.
Here’s a quick look at the highlights. For full details, settings, and screenshots, see What’s New in RustRover 2026.3.
Download RustRover 2026.3
                                                    
Run and review your agents’ work in JetBrains Air
JetBrains Air works with the agents you already use, including Claude Agent, Codex, Gemini, GitHub Copilot, Junie, OpenCode, and other ACP-compatible agents. Your existing subscriptions and API keys carry over, with no JetBrains AI subscription required. Junie Lite gives you a free agent with just a JetBrains Account, and Junie can also work with models running locally through Ollama or LM Studio. When an agent makes changes, you can review them with the surrounding code in view and anchor notes to specific lines in the diff, so the agent knows exactly what to fix.




Read debugger views at a glance
Long, fully qualified Rust names can crowd the debugger. RustRover now shortens type names in the Variables and Watches views and symbol names in the Frames view, so the program state and the call stack are easier to scan. Shortening is on by default, and you can turn it off in the settings.




Go from profiler results to the code behind them
When profiler results point you to a hot spot, Jump to Source now opens the Rust function behind it instead of reporting Declaration not found. Function names in the results are readable instead of mangled. Both improvements work with perf on Linux and DTrace on macOS.




Let agents use the debugger
RustRover now provides a debugger MCP server and a rustrover-debugger skill that teaches agents how to use it. Instead of stepping through the code yourself, you describe the problem in natural language and let the agent collect the runtime evidence: set breakpoints, step through code, inspect variables, and evaluate expressions. This helps you find issues that are hard to spot from the source code and logs alone, such as a value that’s wrong only at runtime. The agent drives the regular RustRover debugger, so you can follow the session and take over at any point.
To get started, enable the MCP server, then enable and install the rustrover-debugger skill for RustRover or your agent of choice. You’ll find the corresponding settings in Settings | AI.




Work on remote machines without leaving RustRover
You can now work on projects hosted on a remote machine directly from RustRover. Connect to a host over SSH, start a development session, and reconnect to it later, all from the IDE. RustRover now uses native OpenSSH, so it works with the authentication methods your team already relies on, including certificate-based authentication, hardware security tokens such as YubiKey, and ProxyJump.




Help us fix what interrupts your work
RustRover 2026.3 automatically sends error and UI freeze reports to JetBrains, so we can prioritize fixes based on their real impact. Reports contain only technical data, and personal details such as file paths, URLs, and usernames are removed before they leave your machine. You can turn automatic reporting off in the settings. For more details, see the FAQ.
More in this release
RustRover 2026.3 also brings these IntelliJ Platform updates:
Sound cues: RustRover can now play sounds when builds, tests, and other background tasks finish, and screen reader users get audio cues for editor line marks. Learn more from this blog post.
Git worktrees: new worktrees now get a copy of your local project configuration.
Plugins page: installed and Marketplace plugins now appear in a single view.
Terminal: the terminal now uses the Ghostty emulator by default for better compatibility with modern CLI tools and terminal-based agents, and you can open terminal tabs in the editor, right next to your code. Learn more from this blog post.
The full list of changes is on the What’s New page.
Try RustRover 2026.3
Update to RustRover 2026.3 or download it from our website, and let us know what you think. Share your feedback in the comments below or in our issue tracker.
Get RustRover 2026.3

posts.title: What’s New in PyCharm 2026.3
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
At the center of this release is JetBrains Air – a new layer for agentic development. It lets you run, track, and verify multi-agent workflows directly inside your IDE, with code intelligence keeping agents on track and complete review tools in your hands. This release also brings workspaces that adapt terminals and consoles to individual subprojects, initial support for Python 3.15 lazy imports, interactive FastAPI dependency graphs, and deeper Pydantic inspections, and so much more.
Download PyCharm 2026.3 now
                                                    
Check out an overview video by our developer advocate William Vincent:






Now, let’s take a closer look at the key highlights.
JetBrains Air in PyCharm – One place to run your agents and verify their work 
As of this release, JetBrains IDEs ship with Air, a new layer for agentic development. Work with the coding agents of your choice, and run, track, and verify multi-agent workflows inside your IDE, where code intelligence helps agents make fewer wrong turns and gives you the tools to review every change before it ships.






Your agents, your models, your subscriptions – with Junie Lite for free
Air works with Claude Agent, Codex, Gemini, GitHub Copilot, Junie, OpenCode, and other ACP-compatible agents. It detects the agents already installed on your machine so you can connect them in a click, and you can add more from the agent registry.
Your existing setup carries over, too: provider subscriptions, API keys, and even a custom base URL all work, with no JetBrains AI subscription required. Run Claude Agent on your Claude subscription in the terminal or in a full-screen IDE tab, use other agent subscriptions in the chat or terminal, and switch between subscriptions at any moment, even mid-session.
Air includes free AI with the Junie Lite configuration, so you can use an agent without a subscription. You only need a JetBrains Account.
A central workspace to review changes and guide the agent
Review an agent’s changes with the surrounding code and your project tools in view, and send feedback straight back to the agent. Anchor a note to a specific line in the diff, or comment directly from the code, so the agent gets concrete context about the change you want. Work in the chat or the terminal, whichever suits you.
Still using AI Assistant? A notification will offer you a trial of Air. Moving to Air hides AI Assistant, if you wish to return to AI Assistant follow the steps outlined here. Air automatically migrates your IDE skills, MCP configuration, agents installed through ACP, authentication, and chat history. Chat mode history isn’t migrated.
Workspace support
A console and terminal for each subproject
Each subproject has its own Python console and terminal running in its own environment, so you run code against the dependencies that subproject actually uses. In uv workspaces, the console uses the workspace environment and adds the subproject root to sys.path.
Right-click a subproject and select Open in | Python console to start a console for it.
Open a terminal while a subproject file is in the editor to run commands in that subproject’s environment.




Subproject creation and conversion
You can add a new subproject or convert an existing folder from the Project tool window context menu. The subproject is initialized using uv, Hatch, or Poetry, and automatically added as a workspace member to your root pyproject.toml in uv workspaces.




Python 3.15 lazy imports
PyCharm now supports the lazy import syntax introduced in Python 3.15. A lazy import defers loading a module until it’s first used, which can noticeably cut startup time in applications and scripts with heavy dependencies. PyCharm parses and resolves lazy imports like regular ones, so you can adopt the syntax without giving up code insight on the names you import.
Learn more about lazy imports in our blog post.




FastAPI support [Pro]
An endpoint can depend on a chain of Depends() and Security() calls spread across many files. PyCharm draws that chain as a graph for any endpoint. Each dependency is marked as yield or return, and circular dependencies, which raise a RuntimeError at startup, are flagged in the editor. In the other direction, a dependency shows which endpoints rely on it, directly or through other dependencies.
You can open the graph from the gutter icon next to an endpoint or click the endpoint count above a dependency to see its usages.




Python interpreter widget
The redesigned Python interpreter widget in the status bar is built around the tools that manage your environments, such as uv, Poetry, Hatch, and conda. It detects the ones installed on your machine and lists the environments each one manages for your project.
Environments created from the command line also appear under their tool. To start working in one, open the widget, select the tool, and pick the environment. To recreate it with a different Python version, choose Recreate Environment under Current Environment. If the Python version you choose isn’t installed, you’ll be prompted to download it.




Pydantic support
PyCharm now provides deeper editor support for Pydantic models. Field constraints, validators, and configuration are read from the model’s declaration and used across the editor.
Values passed to a model are checked against its Field() constraints, such as min_length, max_length, gt, and lt, with a warning displayed when one is broken.
A field name inside @field_validator('price') now resolves to that field’s definition, letting you jump straight to it.
Code completion suggests configuration options in a model’s class arguments, such as validate_by_name and validate_by_alias.




What you see here only scratches the surface of what is included in PyCharm 2026.3. From editing standalone files in the new Home window to full SQLAlchemy ORM support, automatic project configuration copy in Git worktrees, and remote development directly from the IDE via SSH – there is plenty more to explore across code insight, testing, environments, and version control.
Head over to the What’s new in PyCharm 2026.3 page to see the complete list of features, performance improvements, and fixes.
Read the full What’s New
                                                    
We would love to hear how JetBrains Air and the new workspace tooling fit into your day-to-day work – share your thoughts in the comments below or submit feedback directly in our issue tracker.

posts.title: Building a RAG Pipeline for Semantic Code Search: A Developer Diary and Field Notes
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Part 2: Storage, Search, and Agent Tooling 
In this blog series, we aim to share some of the lessons we learned over the past six months as we built and rolled out Air Context, a production-grade RAG system for code search. In the first post of the series, we covered chunking, parsing, and vectorization. Turning code into vectors, however, represents only part of the journey. 
In this post, we’ll tackle the next problems that must be solved for any serious production-grade RAG system: how to store millions of vectors so that the index keeps up with Git, and how to retrieve the right vectors in milliseconds.




Storage
Once we have the code parsed, chunked, and turned into vectors, our next question is where to put them. A real-world codebase can produce millions of vectors. To compound the problem, codebases are not static. Not only do they change often and exist in dozens of branches at once, but the agent expects an answer in milliseconds, filtered down to the right repository, the right path, and only the files that the user is allowed to see. All this requires a special storage layer that efficiently handles the search operations under the given constraints.
At the center of this storage layer sits the vector index. Vector search requires finding the vectors closest to the one representing the query. Comparing a query against a million vectors one by one is far too slow, so in practice we use approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) structures such as HNSW or IVF. These skip most of the comparisons and return results that are very close to the best match, but are not guaranteed to be the best match. That speed comes with trade-offs when it comes to how many of the truly relevant results are actually returned (also known as recall), how much memory the index needs, how well it copes with a constant stream of inserts and deletes, and whether it can respect filters at all.
On top of that, any healthy codebase must support multiple incremental index updates as commits land. To ensure this can happen at scale, the design must avoid keeping a separate copy of every chunk for every branch that shares the same code, and it must maintain consistency for the vectors and the metadata that describes them. None of these capabilities are provided by embedding models. Without strong storage solutions, our painstakingly extracted vectors will simply not be usable.
The role of approximation
Approximate search algorithms sacrifice some measure of recall, but they operate well over a large dataset. 
We found that a hybrid approach, in which we also employ exact search over a more limited vector space following the initial ANN search, works remarkably well.
In other words, using a cheap first pass narrows the whole corpus down to a small set of likely candidates. Running an exact comparison then becomes affordable. The approximate index handles the scale, and the exact pass handles the last mile of precision. This gives us another lever by which to fine-tune the search, as we are thinking not only about which algorithms to use but how to use them in tandem.




Filtered ANN: The nuances
Vector search for semantic similarity is blind to harder search constraints, such as the limitation of results to a repository, branch, or specific subfolder. Additionally, security and permission constraints, such as restrictions on the kind of data that can be queried, must be strictly enforced. This type of metadata filtering needs a deterministic mechanism that will supersede any search algorithm.
Combining a filter with an ANN index is genuinely hard because the two mechanisms fight each other. An HNSW graph is built assuming you can traverse freely between neighbors; the moment you constrain traversal to nodes that satisfy a predicate, the graph can become disconnected and the walk can miss valid candidates. There are three broad strategies to address this:
1. Pre-filtering. This means applying the metadata predicate first, and then searching only the surviving set. It provides 100% recall relative to the filter. However, it loses the ANN index over the filtered subset and effectively falls back to exact search. This strategy is best suited for highly specific filters, such as a single small repo or a narrow subfolder. However, it becomes expensive when the filter still leaves a huge population to search.
2. Metadata bundled with the vector index. The strongest general-purpose approach is a storage that makes filtering a first-class citizen of the index itself. In other words, parameters such as folder permissions or repos are searchable and affect the vector distance. Qdrant and turbopuffer are built this way. You keep most of ANN’s speed *and* honor the filter without falling back to brute force search. For a production codebase RAG with real ACL requirements, this would be a balanced choice.
3. Post-filtering. Run the ANN search first, then throw away results that fail the predicate. The problem, of course, is that because the top-K candidates were not selected with this filter in mind, most or all of them could end up being invalid, leaving you with a short, low-quality list. pgvector’s iterative-scan mode mitigates this by fetching more and more candidates until enough survive the filter, but it carries a cost in latency and can be unpredictable. Post-filtering is considered to be the weakest of the three strategies.
Keeping up with incremental code changes
When working on large code repositories, a RAG system can’t afford to re-index the entirety of the codebase upon every change. Thus, to achieve viable indexing performance and data storage limits, indexing must be performed incrementally.
Ideally, we’d want each repository snapshot to be deterministically clustered into a Merkle tree mirroring its directory structure. New revisions are diffed from the top down, and entire unchanged subtrees are linked to the new snapshot as-is, without any reindexing. The embeddings are further deduplicated by chunk content hash, so within the modified clusters themselves, we would only index the changed code. 
With incrementality in place, index updates and deletions run step by step in small, lock-bounded transactions with limited parallelism, and heavy maintenance such as vector-index builds is offloaded to background jobs, preventing database CPU bottlenecks.




However, all of this processing and business logic costs time and processing resources. Constructing HNSW vector indexes is one of the primary CPU bottlenecks in our database pipeline. To prevent system overload, we decouple vector ingestion from index building. Vectors are written first, and the HNSW index is built only once a repository’s snapshot is fully stored in the database. The build then runs asynchronously under strictly controlled parallelism. To keep CPU usage efficient, we use non-blocking concurrent index creation to allow at most one index build at a time per shard. This keeps the database instances stable, as a snapshot only becomes searchable once its index is ready.
To deal with the CPU, memory, and metadata-capacity limits of a single database instance, our architecture scales horizontally across multiple shards, each backed by its own primary instance and read-only replicas. Search queries are served from the read-only replicas, deployed across geographically distributed regions, to guarantee low latency. Furthermore, to uphold data isolation, each customer is pinned to exactly one shard, with a simple application-side routing layer directing each transaction to the right shard based on the customer identifier. 
Leveraging local indexes for local changes
In a typical SDLC, code is first written on a local laptop or desktop machine, later to be pushed to a remote branch and merged with the rest of the codebase. During these first development stages, that code is highly relevant to the individual developer, but less so to other developers working on their own branches. Creating a local index on the developer’s machine to support the pre-push development stage can help reduce the load and disk requirements from the central search index and ensure the search results are relevant. 
Air Context indexes can live fully on-device to support this use case. For local vector storage and search, we adopted USearch, a compact, high-performance engine built for vectors. Vectors and metadata are separated, with snapshots, clusters, and chunks kept in a dedicated metadata storage alongside the vector index. Because that metadata follows exactly the same model as the server, the entire incremental pipeline keeps working locally. Unchanged clusters are relinked across revisions, and identical chunks share a single stored vector.
Sharing one metadata model between the server and local storage allows us to support cascade indexing, which permits the transition of code from local to shared. Search becomes a two-stage process. First, it runs against the remote index, and then it runs against the local one, using a reranker that merges the top candidates from both sources into a single result list. 
In this manner, we keep a flexible local index that is always synchronized with the local file tree, and at the same time optimize storage and inference by sharing remote indexes for remote branches. Furthermore, we save valuable time by transparently transitioning the index from local to remote as it gets pushed into the central source code.
Post-retrieval optimization
Post-processing: Turning candidates into an answer
The nearest-neighbor search described above does not produce the final result. It produces a list of candidates: the chunks whose vectors sit closest to the query. While this is a great start containing a lot of useful data, it is not the final product to be delivered to the agent or user. The ANN results may contain near-duplicates, several fragments of the same function, or chunks that scored well for the wrong reason, for example because they share a few rare words with the query.
Post-processing encompasses everything that takes place to transform the raw candidate list into the text the agent reads. In our pipeline, this covers removing duplicates, grouping fragments that belong to the same file, deciding how many results are worth showing, and, most importantly, reranking. Each of these steps is cheap compared to the search itself, because each one runs over a few dozen candidates rather than the whole codebase.
Reranking
Reranking can best be described as taking a second, more careful look at the candidates before handing them off. Our first pass has to be fast, since it compares each chunk to the query through two vectors computed independently. A reranker can afford to be slower. Its role is to look at the query and the candidate side by side and judge how well they actually match. While we can’t use an LLM to judge the relevance of results over a massive index, that does become a valid option when dealing with a more limited result set. Ultimately, reranking gives us a reordered list in which the best matches have moved to the top.
In addition to this approach that uses neighbor search followed by reranking, we experimented with several other retrieval configurations. Some of them delivered a noticeable improvement in search quality, but at the price of significantly higher resource use and slower searches. One example is JointRank, a method presented at the ICTIR ’25 conference, which asks a language model to rank many candidates in a single pass by splitting them into overlapping groups, ranking each group in parallel, and combining the partial orderings into one.
Agentic search
Further attempts to improve search quality led us to explore using an agentic search tool. Instead of a single-shot retrieval, we can choose to employ a dedicated code-retrieval agent. This agent can orchestrate calls to several search and read tools, including the embedding-based retrieval. It can make judgment calls on which tools to call and use different thresholds based on the query itself. The agent decides on its own when to search, when to open a file, and when it has seen enough. We cap the number of steps it can take so that exploration never runs away with the budget.
This retrieval agent can be implemented as a sub-agent, a common pattern established in recent years for helper agents that keep an isolated context. When a sub-agent does the reading, only its conclusion comes back, so the main agent’s context stays small and focused. Claude Code, for example, lets users define custom sub-agents that the main agent can call like any other tool. 
A sub-agent can also run on a cheaper or faster model than the one writing the code and can be restricted to read-only tools to prevent it from changing anything by accident. Additionally, several of them can run at the same time on independent questions. For our search tool, this means the main agent spends fewer tokens and less time on finding code and more on the task it was given.
Result formatting and front-loading snippets
A final aspect of the post-processing stage we have to consider is the format we use to hand the results over to the agent. Our goal is to save the agent time by preventing it from making additional calls, while also ensuring it has enough data to assess the relevance of the results for its original goal. This needs to be done judiciously, though, as the more data we front-load into the response, the more we inflate the agent context and possibly pollute it. The strategy we have adopted is to match the level of details to the assessed relevance of each result. 
The results for candidates whose relevance scores exceed a predefined threshold pack more information, including the code chunk itself as well as line numbers and additional metadata. For candidates with a lower estimated relevance, we’ll provide only some basic information like the file name and possibly a very partial snippet. This keeps the agent’s attention on the matches that are likely to be right while still hinting at where else it could look.
From theory to practice
In this post, we discussed the second part of the pipeline, covering storage along with search and retrieval. On the storage side, an approximate index does the heavy lifting, with an exact pass over a small candidate set. Filters for repository, branch, and permissions live inside the index rather than around it. A Merkle-tree view of each snapshot lets the index keep up with Git by reusing everything that has not changed, and a local index on the developer’s machine picks up the work before code is pushed.
On the retrieval side, a reranker takes a second, more careful look at the candidates to judge their relevance. A dedicated sub-agent is capable of a more nuanced exploration when a single-shot search is not enough. Finally, the result format can provide the agent with details in proportion to how confident we are in each match, so the agent’s context stays small and focused.
There’s still one critical line of questioning we haven’t yet addressed: Does any of this actually help the agent? For all of the optimizations, algorithms, and consideration we give to scale, does this RAG apparatus actually make a measurable impact on the agent’s performance? After all, agents, especially when using frontier models, have become increasingly adept at navigating large codebases. With that in mind, what is the added value of semantic search tools? 
These are important questions that have been on our minds from the very beginning of our journey. In the next post, we’ll show how we plug Air Context into agents, what it took to turn it into a product, and how we evaluate it – from retrieval benchmarks to end-to-end agent runs. Spoiler: in those runs, agents with Air Context needed up to 70% fewer turns to solve a task.
As always, ask questions in the comments or share your own hard-won lessons. If you’d like to try it on your own code, Air Context is in public preview and already included with your JetBrains AI subscription.
Until next time!

posts.title: DataGrip 2026.3: Agentic Development With JetBrains Air, Cross-Database Queries, DuckDB Support, and Major UX Improvements
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
DataGrip 2026.3, the third major update of the year, is here! Let’s take a look at what’s inside.
AI
JetBrains Air is now available by default in DataGrip. You can run SQL, explore data, and reference database objects directly in chats with AI agents. SQL snippets use your IDE’s syntax highlighting and formatting settings. You can run them against a selected data source using the Run Query button right in the chat. After execution, you can navigate to object definitions and preview them in the Quick Definition popup. You can view CSV format data in the chat’s data editor with sorting and search options. To reference database objects in your prompts, use @dbObject notation with completion to help you find the object you need. Object references in the chat also support Quick Definition.




UI and UX improvements
First, we’ve moved query results from Services to a new Database Output tool window. It opens automatically at the bottom of the IDE when you run a query, a run configuration, or an SQL file. By default, its contents follow the active editor tab. The header combines the client selector with the Output, Query Plan, and Result tabs. The session client tree is now in a dropdown on the right side of the toolbar, while session management remains in the Services tool window.




Second, we’ve updated the tool window bar in the window header and the default tool window shortcuts. The bar now shows icons for Database Explorer, Database Output, Files, and Agent Sessions by default. For the default tool window shortcuts, Agent Sessions now uses Cmd+2 (macOS) / Alt+2 (Windows/Linux), previously assigned to Files. Files now uses Cmd+4 (macOS) / Alt+4 (Windows/Linux), previously assigned to Run. Run no longer has a default shortcut.




Connectivity
You can now query data across different data sources, even when they use different DBMSs, and view the results directly without copying the data beforehand. To make this possible, we’ve introduced a new Workspace data source, based on DuckDB. In its query consoles, you can use a special syntax to reference and join tables from other data sources, filter them, and also run queries against those data sources.




DuckDB now gets full support, including a dedicated SQL dialect, DuckDB-specific syntax and functions, code completion, and database object introspection. Three connection types are available: default, In-memory, and URL only. The default option connects to a DuckDB database file at the specified path. In-memory creates a database in memory, while URL only uses the JDBC URL you provide as is.




The way DataGrip handles untrusted projects has also been updated. Connecting to a database can execute potentially malicious code, for example, when the connection URL, startup scripts, or driver files have been tampered with. That’s why DataGrip now asks you to trust an untrusted project before connecting to a database. You can also stay in safe mode, where database connections are disabled.




Working with data
Let’s take a look at what’s new in the data editor. We’ve added two buttons to the query results toolbar: Open in Editor Tab and SQL. Open in Editor Tab opens a result set in a separate tab in the main editor area. The action is available for results in the Database Output tool window and for in-editor results.




SQL opens a popup with the result set’s original query. From there, you can run the query again, copy it to the clipboard, or navigate to it in the editor.




Column management also gets a few enhancements. You can now pin columns to the left side of the data editor to keep them visible as you scroll horizontally. You can pin a single column, several selected columns, or all columns up to a selected one.




You can now automatically resize columns to fit the available width of the data editor. This makes it easier to view tables with many columns without adjusting each column individually.




We’ve replaced the Show Column List popup with the new Manage Columns popup. It lets you find columns, select which ones to display, pin or unpin them, and adjust their order in one place. You can also navigate to a column in the grid. Changes to column order and pinning are immediately reflected in the grid. To open the popup, click Manage Columns on the data editor toolbar or press Cmd+F12 (macOS) / Ctrl+F12 (Windows/Linux). Alternatively, right-click a column header and select Manage Columns. An indicator on the toolbar icon shows when some columns are hidden.




Query consoles
We’ve improved transaction control in query consoles. In Manual mode, running COMMIT or ROLLBACK now disables the Commit and Rollback toolbar buttons in PostgreSQL, Greenplum, MySQL, MariaDB, and Oracle. Consoles that share a session also display the same transaction state. We’ve fixed PostgreSQL transaction and savepoint issues and disabled automatic savepoints by default for databases outside the PostgreSQL family.




Database support
We’ve added support for MariaDB sequences and initial support for packages. DataGrip displays them in dedicated sequences and packages groups under the schema node in Database Explorer. DataGrip now introspects packages and their bodies and loads their source code. You can generate their DDL, drop them, and refresh individual packages. We’ve also improved support for package syntax in the code editor.




DataGrip now supports PostgreSQL 19. DataGrip now recognizes INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT ... RETURNING, WAIT FOR LSN, and the EXCEPT clause in CREATE PUBLICATION statements. We’ve updated the minicatalogs to include new PostgreSQL 19 functions, too.




If you’re interested in upgrading to DataGrip 2026.3, or if you have any questions or suggestions, here are a few links you might find useful:
Download DataGrip 2026.3.
Visit our What’s New page for the full list of improvements.
Contact us on X.
Report any bugs to our issue tracker




The DataGrip team
